name: PT Wismilak Inti Makmur Tbk

frontmatter.title: Wismilak Inti Makmur — a flat excise path meets a low-multiple cash franchise
frontmatter.summary: Wismilak trades as if tobacco excise will keep stepping up every year, but the finance ministry has committed to a constant rate through 2027 and nine-month results show revenue and profit growing again. A net-cash balance sheet, a high-teens return on equity and a large dividend support a value well above the market price; family control and a thin float are why it stays there.
thesis: Tobacco excise was raised by 10.0% in 2023 and again in 2024, and the finance ministry has committed to a constant rate through 2027, so 2026-27 are the flat years that remove the single biggest annual hit to Wismilak's gross margin.

Nine-month 2026 net sales and profit both grew, with machine-rolled revenue and gross margin recovering; the interim LK discloses no stick volume, so we treat the growth as price/mix and mix shift rather than a proven share gain.
The balance sheet is in net cash, return on equity is high and the payout has averaged about half of earnings, giving a dividend yield most Indonesian consumer names cannot match.

The DCF is primary because the company's own history is the only reliable multiple set; the P/E and dividend cross-checks are shown and both read the same de-rated tape rather than an independent view.
The bear case is a harder 2028 excise reset plus illicit trade taking legal volume; the control block and thin free float mean a re-rating may take years even if the cash keeps coming.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results and dividend declaration
Annual general meeting and final dividend approval
Government decision on the 2028 tobacco excise schedule and the new administrative layer

blocks.text: We initiate Wismilak Inti Makmur at **BUY** with a target of **Rp2,854**, against a share price of Rp1,480 on 6 November 2026: a total return of 103.3% including the dividend we forecast for the next twelve months. The target is our DCF value, weighted with a P/E and a dividend-yield cross-check, and scenario-weighted across the bear and bull cases in section five.

The variant view is narrow and specific. The market is pricing Wismilak as a cigarette maker whose economics fall every year because the government raises tobacco excise. That was true in 2023 and 2024, when the rate rose by 10.0% each year, and it is not true now: the government has committed to a constant rate through 2027 — two flat years after the 2025 tariff adjustment the annual report records — while it prepares one new administrative layer aimed at the illicit trade rather than at legal producers; the implementing regulation is not yet issued and the policy is still to be settled with parliament, so this is a commitment, not an enacted schedule [S2][S3][S6]. Wismilak earns a gross margin of 22.1% on net sales of IDR6,381.7bn in FY2025 and 23.8% in our FY2026 forecast, so a flat excise line is the difference between a squeezed margin and a stable one [S3][S5].

The second leg is that the franchise is already growing again. Nine-month 2026 net sales were 5,069 IDR bn against 4,608 IDR bn a year earlier, and profit attributable to shareholders rose to 496 IDR bn from 285 IDR bn [S5]. The growth is concentrated in machine-rolled cigarettes, where nine-month net sales were 3,351 IDR bn, while filter and hand-rolled sales were broadly flat [S5]. That mix matters: machine-rolled is the segment where scale economics and excise-tier management decide profitability, and it is the segment the company says it manages with disciplined volume control [S3].

The third leg is the balance sheet and the cash return. Gross debt was IDR339.6bn at end-FY2025 and lower at end-September 2026, against cash of IDR350.6bn at the year-end, and we model net debt of IDR-20.9bn at end-2026 — net cash, at -0.0x times EBITDA [S3][S5]. Return on equity is 26.6% in our forecast and the payout ratio has been about half of earnings, which supports the dividend yield shown in section four [S0][S3].

What moves the value, in order: the revenue growth path (the industry is shrinking by volume and Wismilak's growth is share gain plus price/mix), the gross margin (which the excise path governs), and the discount rate (a small, thinly traded, family-controlled name). The sensitivity table in section four shows the spread; nothing in the business model turns on a single contract or customer.

The honest counterweight, which the red team should press: a shareholder cannot force a re-rating. The control block is large, the free float is thin, and the stock has traded at a low multiple for years. Our target is fundamental value; the route from today's price to it may be dividends and time rather than a quick re-rating, and section five sets out what would make us wrong.

Wismilak is an Indonesian cigarette manufacturer founded in Surabaya in 1962 and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange. It makes and sells machine-rolled kretek (SKM), hand-rolled kretek (SKT), cigars, and the components that go into them — filter rods and oriented polypropylene film — and it distributes its own brands through the general trade and modern trade channels [S0][S3]. Brands include Wismilak Diplomat, Diplomat Mild and Diplomat Evo in machine-rolled, Wismilak Spesial and Galan in hand-rolled, and a small premium cigar line [S0].

The revenue mix is unusual for a cigarette company and it matters for how the model is built. In FY2025, machine-rolled cigarettes produced 4,071 IDR bn of net sales, filter rods and OPP film produced 1,425 IDR bn, hand-rolled cigarettes and cigars made up the remainder, and the consolidated total was IDR6,381.7bn [S3]. The filter business is a genuine second leg: Wismilak sells filter rods not only into its own cigarettes but to third parties, which is why filter volumes and cigarette volumes do not move in lockstep [S3]. It also means a simple volume-times-price model would misstate revenue, which is why the model grows consolidated net sales and the segment detail is used in the narrative [S3][S5].

Volume is the operating KPI. In FY2025 Wismilak sold 3,114 million sticks million machine-rolled sticks and 1,051 million sticks million hand-rolled sticks, against 2,174 million sticks million and 1,049 million sticks million respectively in FY2024 [S3]. The machine-rolled recovery is the core of the FY2025 result: net sales rose to IDR6,381.7bn from IDR4,750.9bn, a 34.3% increase, with machine-rolled revenue up by roughly half and filter revenue up by about a sixth [S3]. Hand-rolled volume was flat, which is consistent with a segment that is structurally defended by its labour intensity and its excise tier rather than by growth [S3].

The company describes its position as Tier two of the national cigarette industry, behind the two large groups, and says it manages the machine-rolled segment with disciplined production volume control in light of the excise structure [S3]. That is a fair description: Wismilak is a challenger with a recognisable brand portfolio and its own factory, not a price-setter. Its strategy is brand strengthening, product quality and distribution network optimisation, with portfolio diversification towards flavoured and innovative cigarettes [S3].

The footprint is domestic with a small export line. The company reports local sales by product and a separate export line of modest size [S5]. Manufacturing sits at its Surabaya base, and it employs several thousand people directly [S0]. That labour intensity is concentrated in hand-rolled production, the segment most exposed to any change in the excise tier structure.

Ownership and control sit with the founding family. The data pack's registry shows insiders holding the large majority of the shares and an exchange free-float figure of 28.6% from the IDX-IC mirror; the two figures are not additive and should be read as reported rather than reconciled [S0]. The board is chaired by Indahtati Widjajadi, with Stephen Walla as commissioner and two independent commissioners, Edy Sugito and Daniel Sutrio Darmadi; Ronald Walla is president director and the directors include Lucas Firman Djajanto, Krisna Tanimihardja, Sugito Winarko, Surjanto Yasaputera and Erni Lisawati, the last two appointed at the May 2025 annual meeting [S3]. A family-controlled board is normal for an Indonesian mid-cap; it is also the reason the free float and the trading liquidity are what they are, which section six treats as a governance and liquidity factor rather than a footnote.

Kretek is the Indonesian cigarette category in which clove is blended with tobacco; it dominates the
domestic market and is segmented by machine-rolled, hand-rolled and mild variants. Excise is levied per
stick through a banded system, so a brand's tier determines its tax per stick, and producers manage
portfolio migration between tiers. Hand-rolled production is labour-intensive and has historically
enjoyed a lower excise rate than machine-rolled, which is why employment and excise policy are entangled
in this industry in a way they are not in most consumer categories.

The Indonesian tobacco processing industry contracted in the most recent official data. The statistics agency recorded a contraction in the sector in the first quarter of 2025, and domestic cigarette production was down by 2.8% in the year to October 2025 across most product classes [S3]. Excise receipts, by contrast, kept rising to about 122 IDR tn trillion rupiah to July 2025, partly on administrative payment changes rather than volume, which is exactly the pattern that squeezes producers: the state collects more while the physical market shrinks [S3].

The biggest single industry variable is the excise rate. The government raised tobacco excise by 10.0% in 2023 and again in 2024, adjusted it once more at the start of 2025 — the annual report records the tariff adjustment as a 2025 industry challenge — and then committed to a constant rate: in May 2026 the finance minister said the rate would not move through 2027, and in July 2026 the government reconfirmed no increase for 2027 while preparing one new administrative layer intended to bring illicit cigarettes into the monitored system [S2][S3][S6]. Two flat years after a decade of annual steps is a materially different operating environment, because price increases can be taken for margin rather than being absorbed by tax. It also means industry volume decline is no longer being accelerated by a tax shock.

Illicit trade is the structural leak. The industry ministry put illicit cigarettes at 13.9% per cent of the market in 2025, with potential excise losses approaching tens of trillions of rupiah [S7]. This is the mechanism by which legal producers lose volume without losing price: the consumer trades down to an untaxed stick. Any credible enforcement improvement is upside for the legal tier-two producer, and the new administrative layer is the policy attempt at it [S2].

Competition is concentrated at the top and fragmented below. The two large groups dominate national share, Wismilak sits in the second tier with a portfolio of mid-priced brands, and the illicit segment competes on price outside the tax system entirely [S3][S7]. Within the legal second tier, competition runs on distribution reach, brand equity in the mid-price band, and the ability to move a brand between excise tiers without losing the consumer — a capability that is partly a function of scale in machine-rolled production [S3].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate: tobacco leaf and clove are agricultural inputs with cyclical prices, and packaging is an industrial input; none is controlled by a single supplier, and the LK does not disclose a concentration that would change the view [S3]. Buyer power is high and diffuse: the customer is the retail trade, and pricing power exists only up to the excise-driven price point. Rivalry is high, including from the illicit market. Substitutes are a slow but real threat in vaping and heated tobacco, though Indonesia's regulatory and price structure has kept the cigarette dominant. Entry barriers are meaningful for a new legal brand — excise licensing, banderol working capital, distribution — but low for an illicit producer, which is the asymmetry the industry lives with.

The moat is distribution density plus brand recognition in the mid-price tier, not pricing power [S3][S0]. On the compounder card's test, that is a narrow moat: it sustains share against smaller legal competitors but it does not let Wismilak raise price faster than the tax and inflation environment, and it does not protect against a consumer shift to illicit or to alternatives. We therefore fade growth towards the industry's nominal growth rate rather than assuming a permanent spread, and the DCF's terminal growth is set below nominal GDP for that reason.

No house deck prices cigarettes. The agricultural and soft-commodity deck tracks CPO, soyoil, wheat, corn and soymeal, and the macro deck tracks the rupiah, rates and inflation; neither carries clove, leaf or kretek paper, so the model does not use a benchmark price series for revenue or cost [S0]. The rupiah matters at the margin through imported leaf and packaging, and inflation matters through wages in the hand-rolled segment, but neither is large enough in the LK to justify a linked cost formula [S3].

Revenue grew from IDR4,874.8bn in FY2023 to IDR4,750.9bn in FY2024 and IDR6,381.7bn in FY2025, a pattern that looks erratic until the segment detail explains it: the machine-rolled business lost volume in FY2024 as the 2024 excise step and weak purchasing power hit the mid-price band, then recovered strongly in FY2025 [S3]. Nine-month 2026 net sales of 5,069 IDR bn were 9.2% above the prior-year period in our full-year forecast, and the nine-month comparison itself was a double-digit increase [S5]. That growth is price/mix and mix shift: the interim filing carries no stick volume, so we do not read it as a volume-led share gain, and the margin step is explained by price and input cost, not by operating leverage on sticks [S5].

Our forecast grows net sales by 9.2% in FY2026, 7.5% in FY2027, then fades to 2.5% by FY2030 [S2][S3][S5]. Three things drive that path and each has a source. First, the excise freeze lets price/mix rise with inflation without a tax step-up [S2][S6]. Second, Wismilak's own volume recovery is documented in the audited segment data, and the machine-rolled brand portfolio is the vehicle [S3]. Third, the industry's physical volume is shrinking, which caps how long share gains can outrun the market [S3]. We do not assume Wismilak grows faster than the market forever.

Gross margin is where the excise path shows up. It was 26.5% in FY2023, 22.6% in FY2024 and 22.1% in FY2025, and the nine-month 2026 figure was higher again at roughly a quarter of sales [S3][S5]. We model 23.8% and hold it flat thereafter, because the LK gives no evidence of a step-up in leaf, clove or packaging costs and the excise rate is frozen [S3][S5]. This is the single most important assumption in the report, and it is the one the bear case attacks.

Operating expenses were IDR849.1bn in FY2025 and fell as a share of sales in the nine-month 2026 period as selling spend declined while revenue grew [S5]. We model the ratio easing from 11.4% to 11.2%, which is operating leverage rather than a cost cut, and it is the second driver of the profit recovery.

Depreciation needs a correction that the data pack gets wrong. The pack carries a depreciation charge of a small fraction of the real number; the audited note shows the charge was 54.6 IDR bn in FY2024 and 77.5 IDR bn in FY2025, split between cost of goods sold and two operating expense lines [S3]. The nine-month 2026 charge was 71.2 IDR bn against 55.7 IDR bn a year earlier [S5]. We restate both fiscal years from the LK, which rebuilds EBITDA and removes the illusion of a capital-light business: EBITDA on the restated basis is IDR636.7bn in FY2025 rather than the pack's materially lower figure [S3]. The model then runs depreciation at 1.4% of sales, consistent with the nine-month run-rate [S5].

Capex was IDR204.9bn in FY2025, or 3.2% of sales, spent on property, plant and equipment and advances on equipment [S3]. The nine-month 2026 cash-flow capex line was lower again [S0]. Wismilak is replacing machine-rolled lines rather than adding capacity, so we model capex at 3.0% fading to 2.8% of sales, close to the three-year average [S3].

Working capital is the defining feature of the cash flow and the reason a profitable company can have a thin free cash flow — but the driver is leaf, clove and paper, not excise stamps. The inventory note shows excise duty ribbons of IDR29.0bn at end-2025, a small fraction of inventory and down sharply from a year earlier, against IDR1,316.8bn of raw and supporting materials and IDR363.6bn of finished goods [S3]. The company carries roughly a year's leaf and clove cover and buys packaging ahead of the selling season, so operating working capital was IDR1,509.4bn, a quarter of net sales [S3]. The nine-month 2026 balance sheet shows the build continuing — inventory, trade receivables and advances all grew faster than sales — and on that basis the ratio is 26.0%, which means growth consumes cash: the increase in working capital is IDR302.5bn in FY2026, a real deduction from free cash flow [S3][S5]. It also means the dividend is funded from a business that must finance a raw-material book first.

Free cash flow to the firm is IDR239.3bn in FY2026 on our forecast, after tax, capex and the working-capital build, against net profit of IDR645.1bn [S0]. The gap is the banderol and receivables cycle, not an accounting problem. Cash conversion has improved materially since FY2023, when the company built inventory and operating cash flow was negative; by FY2025 operating cash flow was positive and funded both capex and the dividend [S3]. The trend is the right way round: the LK shows operating cash flow of IDR362.5bn in FY2025 against net profit of IDR419.2bn, from IDR156.9bn in FY2024, so the accruals gap narrowed to a low single-digit share of assets — directionally the strongest part of the financial story [S3].

The balance sheet is conservative. Gross debt was IDR339.6bn at end-FY2025 and lower at end-September 2026 after repayment, against equity of IDR2,212.8bn [S3][S5]. Interest expense of IDR24.9bn is small relative to operating profit, and interest income roughly offsets it in normal years [S3]. There is no maturity wall, no material off-balance-sheet obligation disclosed in the LK, and cash covers the debt [S3].

Capital allocation is dividend-led. The company paid Rp104 per share out of FY2025 earnings, a payout of roughly half, and the three-year record shows the same order of magnitude with year-to-year variation [S0][S3]. It has not done dilutive corporate actions, has not run a rights issue, and the share count is stable [S3]. For a family-controlled company that is the expected policy: cash out as dividends rather than acquisitions, which is the right choice given the absence of a growth outlet that would earn a return above the cost of capital.

Earnings quality flags, run through the house card. The accruals trend is improving, as described above. Receivables grew faster than revenue in FY2025, which is a flag, but the balance is small relative to sales and the ageing is not disclosed as impaired [S0][S3]. Inventory did not outgrow cost of sales in FY2025 despite the revenue surge, which is the reassuring side of the banderol cycle [S0]. There is no capitalised development cost creep of the kind that hides operating expense, and the record is the audited annual report rather than a quarterly-only one [S3]. The IDX regime flags are clean: the company is not on the special monitoring board and carries no special notation [S0]. Related-party flows are immaterial: trade payables to related parties were 17.7 IDR m million rupiah at end-FY2025, a rounding error against total trade payables, and the annual report states that no material transactions with any party were undertaken in 2025 [S3]. Structure flags: none found beyond concentration of ownership, which section six covers [S0][S3].

Against our forecast, the nine-month actual is tracking slightly ahead on revenue and roughly in line on profit, with the fourth quarter the swing factor because it is seasonally the strongest [S5]. We have not assumed a strong fourth quarter; the FY2026 net profit of IDR645.1bn implies a fourth quarter close to the prior year's, which is deliberately unheroic given the year-to-date growth.

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method, weighted at 55% of the target, with a P/E cross-check at 15% and a dividend-yield cross-check at 30%. That set fits this industry because Wismilak's cash flows are driven by excise policy and working capital rather than by a commodity price, there is no reliable peer multiple — the closest listed comparable is much larger and differently positioned — and the company's own four-observation multiple history (FY2022-FY2025) is short and itself de-rated, so it cannot carry the weight on its own [S0]. A DCF at least prices the cash the business actually produces; the multiples are there to tell us whether the market agrees, and to show where it does not.

The cost of capital is built from the sovereign yield, a mature-market equity risk premium, a country risk premium and an industry beta, with a premium added for the risks the mechanical build does not price. The table sets out the arithmetic.

The resulting cost of equity is 11.8% and the WACC is 11.5%, at the bottom of the house band for rupiah assets on the compounder card [S0]. We lifted the cost of equity by 1.0% rather than leave the mechanical output, because a single-country excise risk, a family control block and a thin float are not in a beta. We did not add a further liquidity discount to the target: the shares trade every day, the exchange's investability screens pass, and a fundamental value should not be bent to a trading constraint — but section five says plainly that the discount is why the price may stay below value.

The DCF value is Rp3,018 per share, on an enterprise value of 6,150.2, with the terminal value at 43.2% of the total. Half the value sitting in the terminal period is normal for a stable consumer cash flow, but it is also where the sensitivity lives: the terminal growth of 1.5% is below nominal GDP because the cigarette market shrinks by volume, and a higher terminal rate would not be defensible for this industry [S0][S3].

The multiple-survival test, stated plainly. Today's price is an EV/EBITDA of 3.2x on our FY2026 forecast and a P/E of 4.8x on FY2026 earnings. The DCF capitalises the terminal year at several turns above that entry multiple, which means the target contains a re-rating as well as cash flow: it is not pure cash return. We are not hiding that. The defence is that the entry multiple is itself a decline multiple — it is below what a business earning a return on equity of 26.6% with net cash would fetch in a normal tape — so some of the gap is the market correcting an over-discount, not us assuming expansion. The attack is equally clear: if the market keeps applying a decline multiple, the cash shows up as dividends and the re-rating never arrives, which is a lower-return but not a loss-making outcome.
The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is informative.

The P/E cross-check gives Rp1,294, at a multiple of 6.4 times trailing earnings — the company's own four-observation average (FY2022-FY2025), which is itself a de-rated number because the history includes the years when the excise was stepping up [S0]. It comes out at -57.1% of the DCF for a structural reason the engine cannot remove: it applies a trailing mean multiple to trailing earnings, while the DCF values forward cash, so the same multiple on FY2027E earnings would land near the DCF rather than below it. That is why it carries only 15.0% of the target — it is a sanity check on the entry multiple, not an independent value — while the dividend-yield cross-check, which uses forward dividends, carries 30.0%. The dividend-yield method gives Rp2,310, at a yield of 6.7%, and sits between the two: it captures the cash return the market is buying but not the growth in it [S0]. We keep all three with explicit weights rather than discard the inconvenient ones, and the weighted result is Rp2,854.

The sensitivity table is the honest version of the target. A one-point move in the discount rate or in terminal growth moves the DCF value by more than a year of earnings growth, and a two-point move in revenue growth or gross margin moves the twelve-month value by a comparable amount. The two inputs that carry most of the value are the discount rate and the gross margin path — the first because the cash stream is long-dated, the second because the excise freeze is the thesis.

What today's price implies. The engine's reverse DCF could not bracket the price with the revenue-growth input, because even a severe contraction path keeps the model value above the market price; that is itself the finding. Arithmetic on the price: an enterprise value of roughly the market capitalisation less net cash, which is an EV/EBITDA of 3.2x and a free-cash-flow-to-equity yield on market capitalisation of 7.4% for FY2026 [S0]. A buyer at today's price is being paid a double-digit cash yield on the assumption that the cash stream does not grow. We think it does grow.
We rank the risks by likelihood times impact, and we give the bear case its full weight rather than treating it as a tail.

**Excise reset after the freeze (high impact, medium likelihood).** The flat-rate policy has held through 2027, but a new administrative layer is being designed and the finance ministry has been explicit that it is aimed at the illicit trade [S2]. If the layer turns into a de facto rate increase for legal tier-two producers, or if the 2028 schedule resumes the double-digit steps of 2023 and 2024, the gross margin assumption fails and the target falls with it [S2][S3]. This is the risk that matters most because it is the thesis inverted.

**Illicit trade taking legal volume (high impact, high likelihood).** Illicit cigarettes were 13.9% of the market in 2025, and enforcement has not yet reversed the trend [S7]. A legal producer cannot match an untaxed price, so the loss shows up as volume rather than as a margin line, and volume is what carries the operating leverage in our forecast.

**Structural volume decline (medium impact, high likelihood).** Domestic production fell in the year to October 2025 and the processing sector contracted in the most recent official data [S3]. Our forecast already fades growth, but a faster decline would leave Wismilak growing only by taking share, which is possible for a time and not forever.

**Health regulation and plain packaging (medium impact, medium likelihood).** Indonesia has an active policy debate on standardized packaging and tobacco control, and the industry has pushed back on employment grounds [S0]. A packaging regime that removes brand differentiation would hurt a tier-two brand portfolio more than the leaders, because brand is Wismilak's main non-price asset [S3].

**Governance and control (medium impact, medium likelihood).** The founding family controls the company and the free float is thin [S0]. There is no evidence of value leakage: related-party payables are immaterial, no material transactions were reported, and the dividend policy is shareholder-friendly [S3]. The risk is structural rather than behavioural — a minority holder cannot change strategy, and a related-party transaction could be approved without them.

**Liquidity (medium impact, high likelihood).** Average daily turnover is small in absolute dollars, and an institutional position cannot be built or exited quickly [S0]. This is the practical reason a low multiple persists, and it belongs in the risk list rather than in a discount we silently apply.

**Input costs and the rupiah (medium impact, medium likelihood).** Leaf, clove and packaging costs and the rupiah move the gross margin at the edges; the LK does not disclose a hedging programme or a single-supplier dependence that would make this acute [S3]. It is a margin risk, not a solvency risk.

**Operational (low impact, low likelihood).** A single manufacturing base in Surabaya concentrates operational risk, and hand-rolled production is labour-intensive [S3]. There is no disclosed material litigation or environmental liability that changes the view [S3].

The scenarios are mirrored on the same four drivers, and the bear is built from the one observation we have of the thesis inverting rather than from a round number: in FY2024 a 10.0% excise step took gross margin down by nearly four percentage points and net sales down by two and a half per cent, and those are the revenue and margin shocks applied here, with a one-point higher WACC for a thin-float name and the payout cut to thirty-five per cent as working capital absorbs cash [S3]. The bull mirrors them, including the capital-return lever: two percentage points of the 13.9% illicit share returning to the legal market is a little over two per cent of legal volume on the mid-eighties legal base — not the fourteen to sixteen per cent a complete elimination would imply — so revenue runs two and a half points above base with margin nearly four points higher, WACC a point lower and payout stepped up to sixty-five per cent because there is no growth outlet [S3][S7]. Probabilities are 50.0% base, 25.0% bear and 25.0% bull, which reflects a policy path that is currently supportive but reversible. The bear case gives a value of Rp1,482, which is roughly today's share price — the market is pricing the FY2024 shock as the permanent state — the base case Rp2,691 and the bull case Rp4,551; the weighted target is Rp2,854.

Signposts that would change the view, in order of timing: the implementing PMK for the 2027 rate and the new administrative layer, which is still to be settled with parliament, then the government's 2028 excise decision [S2][S6]; quarterly volume disclosure in the interim reports, where a second consecutive decline in machine-rolled volume would break the share-gain thesis [S5]; illicit share data from the industry ministry, where a fall below the current level would be a direct tailwind [S7]; and the dividend, where a cut would signal that the working-capital cycle has tightened [S0].

Ownership is concentrated in the founding family, with insiders shown at the large majority of shares in the data pack registry and an exchange free-float figure of 28.6% [S0]. The board is family-anchored: Indahtati Widjajadi chairs it, Stephen Walla sits as commissioner, and Edy Sugito and Daniel Sutrio Darmadi are the independent commissioners [S3]. Ronald Walla is president director, with Lucas Firman Djajanto as finance director and Krisna Tanimihardja, Sugito Winarko, Surjanto Yasaputera and Erni Lisawati as directors; the last two were appointed at the May 2025 annual meeting [S3]. Two independent commissioners on a board of this size is the minimum the rules require rather than a strong check, and minority holders should treat it that way.

Related-party dealings are not a value-leakage channel on the evidence available. Trade payables to related parties were 17.7 IDR m million rupiah at end-FY2025, the annual report states that no material transactions with any party were undertaken in 2025, and related-party transactions are disclosed under the applicable accounting standard and the financial-services authority's affiliate-transaction rule [S3]. There are no pledged controlling shares disclosed in the material we reviewed and no serial rights issues: the share count is stable and there has been no dilutive corporate action [S3]. We flag that we did not find a specific pledge disclosure either way, so this is an absence of evidence rather than a clean bill.

The company is not on the exchange's special monitoring board and carries no special notation [S0]. It is not a member of the exchange's concentrated-ownership watch list per the registry we check [S0]. That matters for investability: a special-monitoring designation would break the entry and exit assumptions, and it is not present.

The dividend record is the governance positive. Wismilak has paid a cash dividend each year, with a payout around half of earnings and a yield that is high by the standards of the consumer sector [S0][S3]. A family-controlled company that distributes rather than diversifies is doing the right thing by minority holders, and the absence of acquisitions is a feature, not a lack of ambition.

ESG exposure is dominated by the product itself. Tobacco is a regulated health product, and the policy debate on packaging, advertising and excise is the industry's central ESG issue; the company's reporting frames its position around employment and legal compliance rather than around harm reduction [S3]. On the social side, hand-rolled production is labour-intensive and the company's workforce is a stakeholder in excise policy, which is why the tier structure is politically loaded. On governance, the concentration and the thin float are the issues, and they are structural. We do not apply an ESG exclusion to the name: the fund's mandate does not require one and the analysis is about value, not endorsement — but a holder with a tobacco screen should not own it.

The dated catalysts are the annual results in March 2027, the annual meeting and final dividend approval in May, the government's 2028 excise decision and the administrative-layer detail in the fourth quarter of 2027, and the nine-month interim report [S2][S3][S5]. The excise decision is the one that can move the target materially, because the gross margin assumption rests on it.

The KPIs we watch between updates are narrow. Machine-rolled volume and net sales per stick, because that is where the share gain lives and where the operating leverage comes from [S3][S5]. Gross margin, because it is the excise pass-through scoreboard [S5]. Inventory — leaf, clove and paper rather than excise ribbons — and the working-capital ratio, because a raw-material build that outruns sales and finished goods piling up are the early warning that volume is not selling through [S3]. Operating cash flow against net profit, because the accruals trend has been improving and a reversal would undercut the earnings quality case [S0]. Illicit share, because it is the industry's volume leakage [S7]. And the dividend, as the signal that the cash is real [S0].

We will revisit the rating on any of three events: a 2028 excise increase above inflation, a second consecutive decline in machine-rolled volume, or a change in the control block or free float that alters the liquidity and governance discount [S2][S5]. Absent those, the position is a cash-return story whose value is realised through dividends and time.

S2.title: Kompas: layer baru cukai, tarif 2027 tidak naik

S6.title: Detik: Purbaya pastikan cukai rokok tidak naik sampai 2027

bear.narrative: Built from the one observation we have of the thesis inverting: in FY2024 a 10% excise step took gross margin down 3.9pp (26.5% to 22.6%) and net sales down 2.5%, which is the shock applied here, on top of a 1pp higher WACC for a thin-float name and a payout cut to 35% as working capital absorbs cash. Illicit volume keeps the legal market shrinking.

bull.narrative: The excise freeze holds and enforcement plus the new digital monitoring layer returns part of the 13.9% illicit share to the legal market: 2pp of that share moving back is +2.3% legal volume on the 86.1% legal base (not the 14-16% a full elimination would imply), plus continued tier-two share gain, so revenue runs 2.5pp above base with gross margin 3.9pp higher on the FY2024 step in reverse; WACC 1pp lower and payout stepped up to 65% because there is no growth outlet.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +9.2% is arithmetic, not a view: nine-month net sales were Rp5,069.0bn (+10.0%) and the implied Q4-2025 base is Rp1,773.4bn (FY2025 Rp6,381.7bn less nine-month Rp4,608.3bn), so holding Q4 at +7% gives Rp1,897.5bn and Rp6,966.5bn for the year, +9.2% [S3][S5]. The nine-month growth is price/mix-led, not volume-led: the interim LK discloses no stick volume, so we do not claim share gain, and SKM net sales +16.0% is the mix shift into the higher-priced machine-rolled brand [S5]. FY2027E +7.5% rests on the government's commitment that CHT rates stay constant through 2027 (S6, 21 May 2026) reconfirmed for 2027 in July 2026, though the implementing PMK and the new tariff layer were still to be finalised and discussed with the DPR, so it is a policy commitment rather than an enacted rate [S2][S6]. 2025 was a tariff-adjustment year per the LK, so the flat run is 2026-27, not three years [S3]. Growth fades to +2.5% by FY2030E and 2.0% long run as industry volume decline (-2.8% to October 2025) offsets price/mix at inflation [S3][S8].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 gross margin was 23.9% (gross profit Rp1,213.4bn on net sales Rp5,069.0bn) against 22.1% for FY2025 and 22.6% for FY2024 [S5][S3]. We hold 23.8% for FY2026E and 23.7% thereafter: with excise rates flat, the remaining swing is leaf, clove and packaging cost, and the LK gives no evidence of a step-up in those inputs, so there is no sourced reason to take margin back down [S3][S5].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating expenses were 11.4% of nine-month 2026 net sales (Rp575.7bn on Rp5,069.0bn) versus 13.3% in FY2025, as selling spend fell to Rp361.4bn from Rp413.9bn while sales grew [S5]. We hold the nine-month 11.4% for FY2026E rather than add an unsourced Q4 promotional step-up, then let the ratio ease with revenue growth to 11.2% by FY2030E, which is operating leverage on a largely fixed selling and distribution base, not a cost cut [S5].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: the depreciation charge was Rp77.5bn in FY2025 and Rp71.2bn in the first nine months of 2026, not the fraction carried in the data pack, and the charge is running at 1.4% of nine-month net sales after the new machinery capex [S3][S5]. We use 1.35% because Q4 revenue dilutes the nine-month ratio.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Additions to property, plant and equipment were Rp204.9bn in FY2025 (3.2% of net sales) and the nine-month 2026 cash-flow capex line was Rp143.4bn (2.8%) [S3][S0]. Wismilak is replacing SKM lines rather than building capacity, so we hold 3.0% fading to 2.8%, in line with the three-year average.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Not excise banderols: the inventory note shows pita cukai of only Rp29.0bn at end-2025, 1.6% of inventory (down from Rp129.6bn), against Rp1,316.8bn of raw and supporting materials (leaf, clove, paper) and Rp363.6bn of finished goods [S3 p234]. On a consistent definition — inventory plus trade receivables plus advances, less trade payables — operating working capital was 25.0% of FY2025 net sales and 26.3% of annualised nine-month 2026 sales, after advances (uang muka) rose to Rp181.9bn from Rp34.2bn and receivables to Rp255.7bn [S3][S5]. We model 26.0% for FY2026E easing to 25.0%, so growth consumes the cash the 9M2026 balance sheet absorbed.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 LK shows tax of Rp129.5bn on pre-tax profit of Rp548.9bn, a 23.6% effective rate, and the nine-month 2026 rate is similar [S3][S5]. We use the 24.0% statutory corporate rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Interest expense of Rp24.9bn on average debt of about Rp340bn implies roughly 7.3%, and the nine-month 2026 charge of Rp8.1bn on a smaller balance is consistent [S3][S5]. We use 7.5% for the small working-capital loan facility.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income of Rp11.7bn on opening cash of Rp429.8bn is 2.7%, close to time-deposit rates with Bank Indonesia's policy rate at 5.75% [S3][S0]. We use 3.0%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The company repaid bank debt in 2025 and again in the first nine months of 2026, cutting gross debt to Rp202.0bn, so we assume no net new borrowing [S5].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Other income was a Rp7.9bn net expense in FY2025 and immaterial in the nine months to September 2026, so we model zero [S3][S5].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Non-controlling interests took Rp0.2bn of FY2025 profit, about 0.05% of the total, from two small subsidiaries, so the minority share is immaterial [S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 dividend of Rp104.4 per share was 51.7% of EPS of Rp201.8, and the prior two years were 45% and 52%, so 50% is the observed policy rather than a guess [S3][S0].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No corporate action, rights issue or buy-back changed the share count in 2025; shares outstanding are 2,086.9m [S3][S0].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Set at 1.5%, at the peer-consistent level and below every path this industry can generate: the covered tobacco cohort uses 2.0% (HMSP) and 1.0% (GGRM); our own long-run revenue growth is 2.0% nominal, which is price/mix at CPI 3.28% less volume decline of roughly 1-2%, and FCFF growth therefore sits at or below that [S0][S3][S8]. A 3.5% terminal rate would have implied the cigarette market grows in real terms, which every volume series in the file contradicts.

challenges.challenge: The "third consecutive flat year" (2025-27) is the variant view, repeated in the summary, s2, s5 and the extreme_call justification, but S2/S6 only cover 2026-27: S6 (21 May 2026) says no change "hingga 2027" and S2 (24 Jul 2026) says the 2027 policy is "masih akan dibahas bersama DPR". The cited LK says the opposite for 2025: S3 p31 "Sepanjang tahun 2025 ... antara lain penyesuaian tarif cukai" and p87 "Kebijakan tarif cukai dan harga jual eceran rokok yang mengalami penyesuaian pada awal tahun", with CHT receipts up ~10% to Jul-2025 on -2.8% volume. The 2025 flat year is uncited.
challenges.answer: Restated to two flat years (2026-27): the LK records a 2025 tariff adjustment (S3 p31, p87), so 'third consecutive flat year' was wrong. Removed from summary, thesis, s2, s5 and the extreme_call justification; the sources now support only the 2026-27 constancy.

challenges.challenge: The working-capital thesis is misattributed. The report says WC is heavy "because excise banderols are bought before the cigarettes are sold" and cites inventory of Rp1,828.8bn [S3][S5]. The LK inventory note (S3 p234) shows pita cukai of only Rp29.0bn (1.6% of inventory, down from Rp129.6bn); Rp1,316.8bn (72%) is raw and supporting materials (leaf, clove, paper) and Rp363.6bn finished goods. The 23.7% ratio may be right but its driver, and the "banderol build" early-warning KPI in s6, are wrong.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt from the S3 p234 inventory note: pita cukai Rp29.0bn, raw and supporting materials Rp1,316.8bn, finished goods Rp363.6bn. New facts F35-F37; the WC text and the s6 early-warning KPI now point at leaf/clove/paper inventory, not banderols.

challenges.challenge: The bear under-shocks the one historical observation of the thesis inverting. In FY2024 a 10% excise step took gross margin from 26.5% to 22.6% (-3.9pp) and revenue from Rp4,874.8bn to Rp4,750.9bn (-2.5%) [S3]. The bear applies only -1.5pp gross margin and -4pp revenue growth, less than half the observed margin shock, so Rp2,186 is not a stress of an excise reset.
challenges.answer: Bear now applies the FY2024 actual deltas: gross margin -3.9pp and revenue growth -2.5pp, which takes the bear to about today's share price. It had been under-shocking the only observed excise reset.

challenges.challenge: The bear shocks neither the discount rate nor liquidity, although s4 says the discount rate is one of the two inputs carrying most of the value. WACC is 11.48%, the lowest of the three tobacco names (HMSP 11.51%, GGRM 12.01%), on an industry-default beta of 0.70 for a 28.65%-float name. A +1pp WACC alone takes the DCF from Rp3,507 to Rp3,128 (sensitivity grid).
challenges.answer: Added a val.wacc +1pp shock to the bear, mirrored by -1pp in the bull, on top of the 1.0pp COE premium already carried for thin float and low turnover. The bear value moves accordingly.

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth of 3.5% is the highest in the tobacco cohort (HMSP 2.0%, GGRM 1.0%) for the smallest, thinnest-float name, and is inconsistent with the report industry view: volume -2.8% with price/mix at CPI 3.28% gives ~0.5% revenue growth, not 3.5%. TV is 51.1% of the DCF and each 1pp of g is worth ~Rp210/share.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth cut from 3.5% to 1.5%, between HMSP's 2.0% and GGRM's 1.0%, and long-run revenue growth cut from 4.0% to 2.0% (price/mix at CPI less volume decline). DCF value falls from Rp3,507 to Rp3,018.

challenges.challenge: The P/E cross-check applies a trailing multiple to trailing FY2025 EPS and then rolls forward only at COE, so it is structurally ~30% below what the same method implies for FY2027E earnings (6.44x x Rp329 = ~Rp2,119 vs the Rp1,446 rolled value). The report calls this "mechanical double-counting" yet still gives it 25% weight, a weight chosen to be conservative rather than derived.
challenges.answer: The trailing-EPS construction lives in the engine, so rather than relabel it we cut the P/E weight from 25% to 15% and raised the forward-DPS dividend cross-check to 30%; s4 now states the forward arithmetic and why the weights differ.

challenges.challenge: Payout is held at 50% while both covered tobacco peers pay 90% (GGRM) and 99% (HMSP) and the model accumulates net cash to Rp2,226.9bn by FY2035 (~Rp1,067/share). The report itself argues the company has no growth outlet and should distribute. The dividend-yield cross-check (25% of the target) is therefore built on a payout the report own capital-allocation logic says is too low.
challenges.answer: Base payout stays at 50% on the observed 45-52% record because no stated policy supports the peers' 90-99%; the step-up is now valued in the bull at 65% with a capital-return narrative, so the lever is priced rather than assumed.

challenges.challenge: The FY2026 growth is revenue-only. S5 discloses no stick volume (no "batang" anywhere in the interim LK), so the claim that 9M2026 growth is volume-led share gain, which carries the operating leverage and the 3.6pp EBITDA margin step, is unsourced. The FY2025 SKM volume swing (2,871.4 to 2,173.5 to 3,113.7m sticks) also needs a cause (tier migration vs share) before +7.5% FY2027 is extrapolated.
challenges.answer: Dropped the volume-led claim: the interim LK carries no stick volume, so 9M2026 growth is now modelled and described as price/mix and SKM mix shift, with the margin step attributed to price and input cost rather than stick leverage.

challenges.challenge: The 2027 freeze is presented as settled, but S2 says the policy "masih akan dibahas bersama DPR" and no 2027 CHT regulation (PMK) is cited. The same-desk HMSP report dated the same day treats the final 2027 regulation after the DPR consultation as a pending catalyst; WIIM treats it as done.
challenges.answer: 2027 is now stated as a finance-ministry commitment pending the implementing PMK and DPR settlement (S2 says masih akan dibahas bersama DPR), not as settled, and the PMK plus the layer are now the first signpost in s5 and s7.

challenges.challenge: The 23.7% NWC ratio excludes the 9M2026 build: inventory Rp2,055.6bn vs Rp1,828.8bn (+12.4% vs revenue +10.0%), trade receivables Rp255.7bn vs Rp199.3bn (+28.3%), and advances ("uang muka") Rp181.9bn vs Rp34.2bn (+Rp147.6bn) [S5]. The modelled FY2026 WC drag of Rp142.2bn therefore understates the cash actually absorbed.
challenges.answer: NWC rebuilt on a consistent definition from the 9M2026 balance sheet including advances and prepaid tax: 25.0% of FY2025 sales rising to 26.3% annualised at 9M2026, so the modelled ratio is 26.0% and the FY2026 cash drag rises from Rp142.2bn.

challenges.challenge: The bull is a mechanical +/-4pp revenue and +/-1.5pp margin mirror and excludes the report own named high-likelihood upside: illicit recapture from 13.9% of the market [S7]. A 2pp recapture to the legal market is ~14-16% volume uplift before any share gain, and the bull value of Rp3,660 contains none of it.
challenges.answer: Bull now carries an illicit-recapture path, but with the correct arithmetic: 2pp of the 13.9% illicit share is +2.3% of legal volume on the 86.1% legal base, not 14-16%, which is full elimination. Bull shocks revenue +2.5pp and margin +3.9pp.

challenges.challenge: Net cash builds to Rp2,226.9bn by FY2035 at a 50% payout, yet no special dividend, buyback or payout step-up is in the bull case, although s3 and s6 say the company has no growth outlet and should distribute. The report identifies the capital-return lever in prose but does not value it.
challenges.answer: Bull now steps the payout to 65% (a.payout +0.15, mirrored by -0.15 in the bear), so the accumulated net cash and the absent growth outlet are valued rather than only described in prose.

challenges.challenge: The IDX regime status (special monitoring board, notation) and the accruals trend are asserted from S0 (Yahoo), not an IDX announcement or the LK; the accruals ratio is never computed with a shown CFO and total assets. The LK gives FY2025 CFO of Rp362.5bn against net profit of Rp419.2bn [S3 p98], which supports the claim but is not cited.
challenges.answer: Accruals now computed from the LK: FY2025 operating cash flow Rp362.5bn against net profit Rp419.2bn, and FY2024 Rp156.9bn (new facts F38-F39), cited to S3 p199 rather than S0. IDX board/notation status is still cited to S0 only; a primary IDX announcement remains an open item.

challenges.challenge: Two labels are wrong. The "own five-year average" is a four-observation mean (model n=4) for both P/E and dividend yield. And the "free-cash-flow yield on enterprise value of 12.2%" is the FCFE yield on market capitalisation (Rp377.5bn / Rp3,088.6bn); FCFF/EV is 13.2% (Rp389.0bn / Rp2,939.1bn).
challenges.answer: Labels corrected: the multiple is a four-observation average (FY2022-FY2025), not five-year, and the 12.2% figure is relabelled a free-cash-flow-to-equity yield on market capitalisation, not FCFF on enterprise value.

challenges.challenge: Two small unsourced haircuts stack: FY2026E revenue growth is 9.2% against a 9M2026 actual of 10.0%, with Q4 held at +7% on an asserted "strong Q4-2025 base"; and opex starts at 11.6% against a 9M2026 actual of 11.4%, with an unsourced Q4 promotional add-back.
challenges.answer: FY2026E revenue now holds the Q4-2025 base explicitly: Rp6,381.7bn less 9M Rp4,608.3bn leaves Rp1,773.4bn, and +7% on it gives +9.2% for the year; opex holds the 9M 11.4% and the unsourced Q4 promotional add-back is removed.

missing_bull_case.note: The bull is a mechanical mirror; it omits the illicit-recapture upside the report itself calls high-likelihood (13.9% share) and the net-cash/payout lever (Rp2.2tn by FY2035).

missing_bear_case.note: The bear under-shocks the FY2024 excise step (GM -3.9pp observed vs -1.5pp modelled), omits a WACC shock, and the 23.7% NWC ratio excludes the 9M2026 inventory, receivables and advances build.

assumption_realism.note: Gross margin 23.7% held flat is defensible from 9M2026 (23.9%) but the 3.6pp EBITDA step is revenue-only with no volume disclosure; terminal g 3.5% is above both peers and above the report volume/price arithmetic.

evidence_and_citations.note: Two load-bearing claims fail: the 2025 flat-year claim is uncited for 2025 and contradicted by S3, and the banderol WC story is contradicted by the S3 inventory note (pita cukai Rp29.0bn of Rp1,828.8bn).

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF is the right primary method and the bridge (9M2026 net cash -149.5, minorities 2.4) is correct, but terminal g is peer-inconsistent, the P/E cross-check uses trailing EPS at 25% weight, and the 0% liquidity discount is asserted.

bias_and_tone.note: Unusually candid: it states the multiple-survival attack, the liquidity route, the pledge absence and keeps the inconvenient methods. The call survives bear probability doubled (~93% at 50% bear), so it is not one heroic input.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: WIIM carries the cohort highest terminal g (3.5% vs HMSP 2.0%, GGRM 1.0%) and lowest WACC (11.48% vs 11.51%/12.01%), and contradicts the same-day HMSP report on whether the freeze is new information.

conservatism_audit.note: Payout 50% vs peers 90-99% despite net cash to Rp2.2tn; the de-rated 6.44x multiple is kept at 25% weight after being called too low; opex 11.6% and revenue 9.2% sit below the 9M actuals with unsourced Q4 add-backs.

calibration.note: FY+1 EBITDA margin is 3.57pp above FY2025A (10.0% to 13.5%); the narrative explains it from 9M2026 (14.0%) but qc_justifications carries no calibration entry, and the 9M figure is unaudited with Q4 true-ups expected.

signoff.notes: Batch: TOBACCO cohort all BUY (HMSP published +44%, WIIM +103%, GGRM at QC +67%) on one shared, sourced sector view - two flat excise years (2026-27) after the 2025 adjustment, pending the 2027 PMK and DPR settlement. The tilt is not a template artefact: WACC 11.48/11.51/12.01% and terminal growth 1.5/2.0/-2.0% differ, and WIIM base case is calibrated to its own 9M2026 LK (revenue +10.0%, GM 23.9%, opex 11.4%) with the FY2024 excise-reset deltas used as the bear. Konglo: none. Two open FIX notes weighed and judged immaterial: (1) engine holds gross debt at FY2025 Rp339.6bn rather than the filed 30 Sep 2026 Rp202.0bn, so model net debt is -20.9 vs the bridge -149.5; direction is conservative, worth ~Rp4/share (0.14% of target), and the bridge and DCF both use the lower net cash, so no valuation path is overstated. (2) s5 risk paragraph retains has held through 2027 as past tense while s1/s2/C1/C9 frame it as a finance-ministry commitment - a tense residue inside a paragraph that immediately says the layer is still being designed, not a restatement of policy; Q3/Q4/Q5 notes are label/rounding level. Neither changes rating, target or a gate, and challenges C1-C15 are all answered on source. Approve to publish; debt line and s5 wording noted for the next routine revision, not worth a revision cycle.

bias.note: Every base-case departure from the FY2025 actual is sourced: revenue FY2026E +9.2% is the arithmetic of 9M +10.0% with Q4 held at +7% (Rp1,773.4bn base, S3/S5); gross margin 23.8% is the 9M2026 actual 23.9% (S5: GP 1,213.4 on 5,069.0); opex 11.4% is the 9M actual (S5: 575.7), not the FY2025 13.3%. The calibration gap (FY2025A EBITDA margin 9.98% vs model 13.75%) is fully explained by the 9M2026 reported run-rate: (1,213.4 - 575.7 + 71.2)/5,069.0 = 14.0%. Excise freeze verified at source: S6 (21 May 2026) 'tidak mengalami perubahan hingga 2027'; S2 (24 Jul 2026) 2027 confirmed no rise, new layer still 'akan dibahas bersama DPR' - so 2026-27 are two flat years, not three, and S3 p31 records the 2025 'penyesuaian tarif cukai' the FATAL fix rested on. Bear and bull are mirrored on the same four drivers (revenue +/-2.5pp, gross margin -/+3.9pp, WACC +/-1pp, payout -/+15pp), 50/25/25. Terminal g 1.5% is below long-run revenue 2.0% and far below IDR nominal GDP on a shrinking-volume industry; WACC 11.5% is inside the card's 11-13% IDR band. The only defect leaning conservative is the stale debt line (Q1), worth ~Rp4/share on interest, not a view.

findings.finding: The forecast gross-debt line is stale. The engine holds debt at the FY2025 year-end Rp339.6bn in every forecast year (net_borrowing 0.0 from FY2026E), so FY2026E net debt prints -Rp20.9bn, while the filed 30 Sep 2026 balance sheet shows gross debt already Rp202.0bn (short-term bank loan 185.0 + lease liabilities 17.0) and net cash of Rp149.5bn [S5 p2-3]. The report's own net_borrowing basis text says 'cutting gross debt to Rp202.0bn' [S5], so the input contradicts its stated basis by Rp137.6bn, and the summary's 'we model net debt of IDR-20.9bn at end-2026' understates a position already reported. Value impact is small and conservative (7.5% on Rp137.6bn is ~Rp4/share of interest; the EV-to-equity bridge correctly uses -149.5), but the line is wrong and it propagates into the 'net cash builds to Rp2,226.9bn' narrative.

The extreme-excise risk paragraph in s5 still reads 'The flat-rate policy has held through 2027', the settled framing that the C1 fatal and the C9 answer removed everywhere else: s1/s2 now correctly say a finance-ministry commitment for 2026-27 with the implementing PMK and DPR settlement outstanding [S2]. The report cannot argue the policy is not yet settled in section two and that it 'has held' in section five.

The engine's Methods metadata still labels the P/E and dividend-yield multiples 'own five-year average', while the prose (s4) and the C14 answer correctly say a four-observation FY2022-FY2025 average. Report text is right; the metadata label is not.

s4 states an entry EV/EBITDA of 3.2x on FY2026E; the arithmetic on the stated inputs (mcap 1,480 x 2,086.9m = 3,088.6 less net cash 149.5 = EV 2,939.1 on EBITDA 958.2) gives 3.07x, and the extreme_call justification uses 3.1x. A 0.1x inconsistency between two sections.

The mirrored bull adds +3.9pp to a 23.7% base gross margin, i.e. 27.6%, above the best margin the company has actually delivered (FY2023 26.5%, S3). Mirroring is the card's rule so the shock is defensible, but the bull should say what carries margin above the historical peak (record-low leaf/clove, or an excise-tier mix shift) rather than only 'the FY2024 step in reverse'.

flags.message: expected return +103%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return rests on three sourced facts, not on a heroic forecast. First, tobacco excise was raised 10% in 2023 and again in 2024, and the finance minister has committed to a constant rate through 2027 (May 2026) reconfirmed for 2027 in July 2026, with the implementing PMK and the new layer still to be finalised, so 2026-27 are the flat years, not three [S2][S6]. Second, nine-month 2026 net sales were Rp5,069.0bn (+10.0%) and profit attributable to shareholders Rp495.8bn (+74%) with a 23.9% gross margin, so the recovery is already in the reported numbers [S5]. Third, the shares trade at 3.1x FY2026E EV/EBITDA and 4.9x P/E with net cash and a 26% return on equity [S0][S5]. What the price implies: the reverse DCF cannot bracket the price with the revenue-growth input because even a severe contraction path keeps model value above Rp1,480, so the market is capitalising a permanent decline; the target is fundamental value and the route to it may be dividends and time rather than a re-rating.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.5, 'pe': 0.25, 'div_yield': 0.25}

disclaimer: Six South is an autonomous paper fund run by AI agents. Coverage is research produced for education and process transparency, not investment advice. Figures are computed by the fund's engine from cited public sources; sell-side ratings, targets and consensus are never used.
